full_judgment:
Mamnoon Rahman J: Zeyad Rahman in Company Matter No. 61 of 2010 and Dr Md Rowshan Ali in Company Matter No. 62 of 2010 are the respective petitioners. In both matters respondent No. 1 is Delta Insurance Company Limited. In Company Matter No. 61 of 2010 Dr Muhammad Rowshan Ali and Md Mojibur Rahman were respectively added as added respondent Nos. 2A and 2B while in Company Matter No. 62 Zeyad Rahman was added as respondent No. 2A. Since the subject matter of both the applications center around the same factual aspects and the same question of laws are involved, both the matters are heard together and being disposed of by this common judgment which will govern both the matters. The facts of these two matters are as follows:

2. Company Matter No. 61 of 2010

The case of the petitioner in Company Matter No. 61 of 2010 in short is that he is a share-holder of respondent No. 1 company, being the beneficiary owner of Account No. 12025300375- 7944; that he holds 8098 (eight thousand ninety eight) share of public shares; that the Respondent No. 1 was scheduled to hold its 19th AGM on 19-9-2005 in respect of financial year ended on 2004 but upon an application, in Company Matter No. 114 of 2005, filed by a share-holders namely Mr AQM Nurul Afsar, this Court, by order dated 31-4-2005, stayed holding of the Annual General Meeting (AGM) of the Respondent No. 1 scheduled to be held on 19-9-2005. Eventually the said Company Matter was dismissed for non-prosecution by order dated 2-3-2010. In the meantime, the holding of  19th to 23rd AGMs of the respondent No. 1 for the financial years ending on 2004-2008 have fallen due and it became imperative for the respondent No. 1 company to hold the AGMs for the said periods. It is stated by the Petitioner that in the event this Court condones the delay in delay in holding AGMs for the aforesaid years, the respondent No. 1 company would need 2 fix a fresh record date as per SCE Notification No. SEC /CMRRCD/ 2008-183 / Admin/03-36 dated 5-10-2009; to constitute an election commission and the share-holders of the company would need to cast vote to elect the directors of the company. It has been stated by the petitioner that pursuant to section 76 of the Insurance Act, Board of Directors of an Insurance company shall comprise of 20 directors, out of which 12 directors ought to be elected from the sponsors, 6 directors to be elected from public subscribers and 2 directors to be elected as independent directors. It has been asserted by the petitioner that the shares issued by the respondent No. 1 are ordinary shares, with equal voting rights ranking pari passu to each other. Since its incorporation, the respondent No. 1 company had issued total 3,00,000 ordinary shares and some of them are yet in script/paper form, while majority share have been converted into script less/electronic shares. Script shares were converted into script less shares following establishment of the Central Depository Bangladesh Limited ('CDBL').

3. All shares are required to be traded through the CDBL system. Approximately more than 60% of the shares from both groups of share-holders have already been dematerialized and merged. The petitioner also asserted that the Insurance Act, 2010 has not taken into cognizance of the Central Depository System ('CDS'), which is run by the CDBL, and CDS does not recognize classification of shares. It is stated by the petitioner that since the respondent No. 1, CDBL or the holders of dematerialized shares themselves are unable to ascertain whether the shares they are holding are either sponsor shares or public shares, and further in the absence of any discrimination between voting rights of all the issued shares of the respondent No. 1, the petitioner and owners of all script less/dematerialized share as well as holders of script shares are entitled to cost vote by way of two separate ballots in the election of directors amongst both the sponsors share-holders and public share-holders as envisaged in section 76 of the Insurance Act, 2010. It has further been stated by the petitioner that he is the holder of the dematerialized shares in his Beneficiary's Account No. 1202530003757944 and as a share-holder of the company, he is lawfully entitled to vote in electing the sponsor and public directors of the said company by two different ballots. The petitioner prayed for the following reliefs:—

i. To condone the delay in holding the 19th, 20th, 22nd and 23rd AGMs of the respondent No. 1.

ii. To direct the respondent No. 1 to hold the said AGMs within a stipulated period of time by fixing a new record date as per SEC Notification No. SEC/ CMRRCD/2008-183.

iii. To direct the respondent No. 1 to appoint a neutral and independent Election Commission comprising of 3 or 5 members, who are not associated with the respondent No. 1 company, for conducting the election of Directors and the election of auditors in the said AGMs of the respondent No. 1.

iv). To direct the respondent No. 1 to invite and allow all share-holders, including the petitioner, to attend and cast votes without discrimination in the election of all directors in two separate ballots.

4. The respondent No. 1, the added respondent Nos. 2A and 2B contented the said application by filing respective affidavit-in-opposition denying material allegations set out in the petition. All these respondents although concurred to the prayer for condonation of delay for holding of the AGMs for the aforesaid years but opposed the consequential directions prayed for by the petitioner. The answering respondents in their respective affidavits-in-opposition in more or less the same terms contended that the board of directors having recommended for the 19th AGM to be held for the year 2004 and the board of directors having fixed book closure and the said date having expired, there is no scope for fixing a new record date for the said AGM in view of SEC Notification No. SEC/CMRRCD/2001-14/24/ Admin/-03 dated 26-11-2011 (Gazetted on 10-12-2001). It was further stated that fixing of record date is a matter that lies the issuer in view of section 2 (Chha) read with section 44 of the Depository (User) Regulation, 2003. The Securities and Exchange Commission also issued another Notification under section 2CC of the Securities and Exchange Ordinance, 1969 conforming that the board of directors of an issuer will fix the record date. It was contended that the fixation of record date is a legal compulsion, which is a duty assignment on the board of directors to discharge the same at the proper time when arrives and the Court may not interfere with regard to fixation of record date in a preemptive manner at a premature stage. It has further been stated by the respondent that the constitution of the Election Commission as prayed for is not permissible under Rules 15B(5), (6) and (7) of the Insurance Rules, 1958 (the said Rules). This concept is foreign to the Companies Act, 1994 as well. It is asserted by the respondents that the Rule, having spelt out the method of appointing Election Commission, this Court should not venture into the appointment of an Election Commission in contravention of the said in as much as, when no case been made out by the petitioner as to the neutrality of the chairman of the board. In the affidavit-in-opposition, it has further been stated that section 76(2) of the Insurance Act, 2010 (Insurance Act) makes it mandatory that the election of the directors shall be conducted as per the Rules prescribed. Relying on section 76(2) of Insurance Act read with Rules 15B(5), (6) and (7) of the said Rules the respondents contended that the prayer for independent election commission is barred.

5. The respondents in the affidavit-in-opposition further stated that section 76 of the Insurance Act, 2010 recognizes of shareholding for the purpose of election of directors. It has been stated by the answering respondents that unless there is sponsor shares, there cannot be any sponsor directors. It has been stated by the answering respondents that according to Rules 15B(1) and (2) of the said Rules, public directors are to be elected by the public subscribers. Article 96 of the Articles of Association provides that the sponsor directors are to be elected by the sponsor share-holders, while the public directors shall be elected by the public subscribers. Therefore, there is no scope for public subscribers to elect sponsor directors and vice versa. The answering respondents categorically stated that the litigations referred to by the petitioner have no manner of relevance with regard to the present management and the petitioner has failed to disclose any real and genuine cause of apprehension to justify his claim for neutral and independent Election Commission for conducting of election of directors or the auditors. It is further stated that the prayer for neutral Election Commission is premature because unless poll is demanded by the share-holders in the Annual General meeting, the question of election does not arise.

6. The petitioner, by filing an affidavit-in-reply, averred that the respondent No. 1 company raised further capital of Taka 1,50,00,000 (Taka one crore fifty lac) only by way of issuing 1,50,000 ordinary shares of Taka 100 each through IPO. At the material time, the share certificates of those ordinary shares were issued in paper/script form. At the time of listing on the Stock Exchange with the IPO, there were only 20(twenty) share-holders acting as promoters/sponsors, who had subscribed to 1,50,000 number of ordinary shares prior to the issuance of IPO.

7. Thus, the ratio of share-holding between sponsors and public was 50: 50 at all material time. All these issued shares were ordinary shares being equal right to dividend, voting participation in the meeting etc, without any discrimination/difference. The Articles of Association of the respondent No. 1, company did not provide for any limitation on the voting rights of the shares subscribed by the share-holders, in particular, in relation to the formation of a new board of directors where all the directors are elected pursuant to the change in law and the fact that AGMs of the company could not be held for the last six years. Therefore, the provision of Article 96 of the Articles of Association that addresses the voting rights of the shares when reelecting retiring directors is not relevant in the instant case. It has further been stated in the affidavit-in-reply that until 30-06-2010, out of total 300,000 ordinary shares as issued by the said company, the total 1,88,088 (one lac eighty eight thousand and eighty eight) shares stood in dematerialized form. Thus, the number of shares in dematerialized form constitutes about 63% of the total issued and paid up capital of the company. This means that the holders of dematerialized shares constitute majority of the share-holders of the company. But due to ulterior motive of the holders of the shares in script form who constitute a minority, the interests of these majority share-holders of electronic shares are at stake and therefore, the petitioner is seeking the protection of the Court through the instant company matter for protecting the best interests of the company.

8. The petitioner in the said reply also stated that once a script share is dematerialized and lodged into the CDS system, any earmarking of 'sponsor' or 'public' share is lost since the CDBL does not have any method of maintaining such distinctions. As a result, even when a dematerialized (i.e. electronic) share is rematerialized into paper form, it is practically impossible for the company to convert the share with certainty as to whether this is a promoter share or a public share.

9. The petitioner, in his reply, by referring to Writ Petition No. 6039 of 2005, Writ Petition No. 4673 of 2006 and Writ Petition No. 4773 of 2007 stated that there has been a history of dispute and mistrust between different directors and share-holders of the respondent No. 1 company, which is very likely to jeopardize a free and fair election of directors of the respondent No. 1 company. The petitioner also mentioned that Company Matter No. 114 of 2005 was filed by one Mr AQM Nurul Afsar, where prayer was made for holding of the AGM under the Chairman of a neutral person appointed by the Court, which however was dismissed for non-prosecution.

10. Company Matter No. 62 of 2010.

Dr Md Rowshan Ali, a share-holder director of the respondent No. 1 company filed application under section 81 read with section 85(3) of the Companies Act, 1994 for condonation of delay in holding AGMs of the respondent No. 1 company for the calendar years 2005-2010. In the application it has been con-tended by the petitioner that one AQM Nurul Absar a share holder of the company filed Company Matter No. 114 of 2005 challenging 19th AGM of the respondent No. 1 company. This Division vide order dated 31-8-2005 in the said Company Matter No. 114 of 2005 admitted the said company matter and stayed the holding of 19th AGM of the respondent No. 1 company. The said Order of stay remained in force until this Court vide Order dated 2-3-2010 dismissed the said company matter for non-prosecution. Thereafter, the petitioner filed the above Company Matter No. 62 of 2010 praying for the following reliefs:—

i. To condone the delay in holding 19th to 24th AGMs of Delta Life Insurance Company Limited i.e. the respondent No. 1 for the calendar years 2005 to 2010.

ii. To allow the Auditor appointed for the calendar year 2004 to audit the financial statement of the calendar years 2005 to 2010.

11. Dr M Zahir, the learned Senior Counsel appearing for the petitioner in Company Matter No. 61 of 2010 submitted that under section 76(1) of the Insurance Act, 2010 in a Insurance Company, the total numbers of directors will not exceed 20, out of which 12 directors will be from sponsor share holders, 6 directors will be from public share-holders and 2 will be independent directors. Dr Zahir submitted that under section 76(2) of the Insurance Act, 2010 the share-holder shall elect the directors in the manner prescribed by the Rules. Dr Zahir, the learned counsel then referred to section 160(Chha) of the Insurance Act and submitted that the Rules framed under Insurance Act, 1938 shall save and limit the same is not inconsistent with the provisions of Insurance Act, 2010 be deemed to have been framed under the said Act of 2010. Dr Zahir relying on Rule 15A and 15B of the said Rules submitted that the said Rules does not recognize sponsor directors to be appointed by the sponsor shareholders. Dr Zahir submitted that Companies Act does not permit classification/categorization of share-holder. He by referring to section 2(40) of the Insurance Act submitted that the words or expressions the definition of which have not been given in the Act of 2010 such words or expressions which have been defined in the Companies Act, 1994 shall be made applicable in all insurance companies. He submitted that since Companies Act does not permit any categorization/classification of share all share-holders shall elect their directors. He then referred to the prospectus for public issue of 1,50,000 ordinary shares (Annexure E).

12. Placing the prospectus Dr Zahir, the learned Counsel further submitted that the prospectus does not reflect any categorization of shares so as to give extra advantage to any group of share-holders in respect of anything including voting rights. He submitted that prospectus is an instrument of representation from the company to the public at large and the ordinary share-holders having acted pursuant to the said prospectus the respondent No. 1 company is stopped from doing anything to their detriment. He also submitted that the prospectus does not create any restriction in respect of voting of an ordinary share-holder toward election of sponsor share-holders.

13. Dr Zahir, the learned Counsel submitted that Article 96 of the Article of Association is totally against the scheme of the Companies Act and security laws and, as such, is ultra virus. He then referred to Regulations 79 and 80 and submitted that those regulations are mandatory in nature in view of section 17 of the Companies Act and whether or not company adopts those regulations; the same shall be treated to have been incorporated in the Articles of Association. Elaborating the scope of the aforesaid Regulations, Dr Zahir submitted that nowhere in the Regulation there is any provision of sponsor share-holders. He also submitted that an aforesaid regulation does not permit voting of difference classes. He submitted that the addition of Article 96 in the same is ultra virus. Dr Zahir, the learned counsel thereafter having submitted a written submission summarized his submission on the following points:—

i. If the Prospectus (Annexure-El filed in the affidavit-in-reply by the petitioner in Matter No. 61 of 2010) of the respondent No. 1 company (that was issued by the Company at the time it was being listed in the Stock Exchange for issuing shares to the public at large) is reviewed then the following can be observed.

The Prospectus categorically provides that each share will have one voting right. It does not provide that the voting right will be limited to the effect that the holders of public shares will not be able to cast vote for election of sponsor directors. The legal effect of a prospectus is that it is a promise made by the company to invite the public to subscribe its shares.

The Prospectus also does not set down any limit in relation to Directors' remuneration and qualification.

ii. Similarly, a review of the provisions of the Article of Association of the respondent No. 1 Company clearly shows the following.

Article 96 (proviso) of the Articles of Association deals with re-electing retiring directors. Article 96 (proviso) cannot override but shall be interpreted as subservient to the mandatory provisions of section 17 and 91(1)(b) of the Companies Act which envisages the directors of the company shall be elected by the members from among their number in general meeting.

Schedule 1, Regulations 80, 81 (dealing with rotation of directors) and 61 (stating that on a show of hands every member present in person shall have one vote of the Companies Act are compulsory regulations also a company cannot limit or qualify these compulsory regulations.

"Therefore, the proviso to Article 96 to the extent it is contrary to or contravenes mandatory provisions of the Act shall be and is ultra virus.

Moreover, Article 96 (provision) of Articles of Association should not be considered for AGMs in question since it deals with re-election of directors only; whereas, due to the application of section 76 of the new Insurance Act, the entire Board will need to be reconstituted (as opposed to being re-elected).

The law is absolutely silent about how sponsor directors will be elected who, by virtue of section 76 of the Insurance Act 2010, would constitute 14 out of 20 Board Members. To sum up, both the old and new Insurance Acts do not specifically deal with how sponsor directors will be elected; they only deal with how public directors will be elected.

Insurance Act and Rules (old law) do not mention sponsor shares. It is only in Article 96 of the Articles of Association, which is in conflict with section 17(2) of Companies Act (which states that creating sections are compulsory sections) and section 91(1)(b) of the Companies Act (which states all members vote for directors equally).

14. Mr Akhtar Imam, the learned Senior Counsel appearing on behalf of respondent No. 2A in Matter No. 62 of 2010 submitted that the respondent No. 1 company and other insurance companies are still, in theory, maintaining share categorization in terms of sponsor shares and public shares. Mr Imam submitted that this categorization has been removed in the backing industry whereas the insurance industries have not yet taken any steps towards de-classification of shares. He submitted that since its incorporation, the company has changed its shareholding structure primarily due to transfer and transmission of shares and listing of its shares in the stock exchanges. The company listed itself in the Dhaka as well as the Chittagong Stock Exchange in the last quarter of 1995. With the establishment of the Central Depository Bangladesh Limited (CDBL), (i) all shares listed in the stock exchange are required to be traded through the Stock Exchange and (ii) shares that are traded through the Stock Exchange are required to be converted into script less/dematerialized form (Directive No. SEO/CMRRCD/ 2009-193 dated 1-6-2010 which states that no paper securities will be traded in the Stock Exchanges from 1-10-2010). As a result of the above, share in script less shares following establishment of the CDBL. Mr Imam the learned counsel also submitted approximately more than 63% of the shares from both groups of share-holders of the company have already been dematerialized and merged. The structure of script form of shares and script less/electronic shares in the respondent No. 1 company as of June 30, 2010 is as follows:—

Share type	Number of shares	Approx % of overall shareholding	Total

Sponsors- Non-Demat (with script)	86,525	28.84%	150000

Sponsors- Demat (without script)	63,475	21.16%

Public- Non-Demat (with script)	23682	7.9%	150000

Public- Demat (without script)	126318	42.12%

Total shares=300000 (three lakh)

15. Mr Imam, the learned counsel further submitted that 21% of the overall shareholding of the respondent No. 1 company are dematerialized sponsor shares and 42% are dematerialized public shares. These are being traded through the Central Depository System (CDS), run by the CDBL. The CDS does not recognize categorization of shares and does not maintain a register by which it can be identified whether any holder of dematerialized shares is holding sponsor or public shares. As a result of the above situation, investors holding shares through the stock market cannot categorize themselves either as share-holders holding sponsor shares or public shares. Mr Imam submitted that the Register of Members of company in question is maintained by the company in the following way.

16. Sponsor share register

The sponsor share register maintained by the respondent No. 1 company includes both the sponsor shares that are held in script/paper format and the sponsor shares that have been dematerialized and are being traded in the CDS. While the names of all the sponsor share-holders and their corresponding holding of paper sponsor shares are listed in detail in the public share register, the number of dematerialized sponsor share being traded in CDS is listed under the folio "06363 CDS A/C" the folio "06363 CDS A/C" in the sponsor share register does not show which share-holders are currently holding what proportion of dematerialized sponsor shares.

17. Public share register

Similar to the sponsor share register, the public register maintained by the respondent No. 1 company includes both the public shares that are held in script/paper format by listing the names of the share-holders and their corresponding holding of script public share and also the number of dematerialized public shares being traded in the CDS under the folio "06363 CDS A/C". Thus the number of dematerialized public shares as stated in the folio "06363 CDS A/C" does not reveal which share-holders are currently holding what proportion of dematerialized public shares.

18. "06363 CDS A/C". In this folio, appearing both in the sponsor share register as well as the public share register, the respondent No. 1 company lists the number of shares that have been dematerialized and thus includes both the dematerialized public shares and the dematerialized sponsor shares. The number of shares listed in the under this folio includes those public shares that have been purchased in the course of trading in the stock market.

19. Mr Imam, the learned Counsel submitted that section 76 of the Insurance Act, 2010 provides that the board of directors of an insurance company shall comprise of not more than 20 directors out of which 12 shall be sponsor directors, 6 shall be public subscriber director and 2 independent directors. He submitted that 60% of the directors of the company, i.e. majority of the directors are required to be sponsor directors. Moreover the majority of the directors of the company are required to elect the 2 independent directors of the company (SEC Order No. SEC/ CMRRCD/2006-158 / Admin/02-06 dated 09-01-2006, Corporate Governance Guidelines), condition 1.2 of which provides that independent non-share-holder directors should be appointed by the elected directors. Accordingly, sponsor shares are in a position to elect 14 directors out of 20 directors of an insurance company, i.e. 70% of the directors of the company. Mr Imam submitted that Article 96 of the Articles of Association of the respondent No. 1 company provides that sponsor share-holders shall re-elect sponsor directors, whilst the public subscribers shall re-elect public directors. However, as a result of dematerializing of the shares, 63% of the shares held by the share-holders of the company from the Stock Exchange are not aware as to whether they are holding sponsor shares or public shares. According to Mr Imam 63% share-holders of the company will not be able to exercise their voting rights for election of directors of the company pursuant to the provisions of the Article 96 of the Articles of Association of the company, which requires that sponsor share-holders be re-elected by sponsor directors and public subscribers re-elect public directors. Mr Imam submitted that respondent No. 1 company in its affidavit-in-opposition has stated that dematerialized share should be treated as public shares and accordingly these share-holders can vote in only for election of public directors. However, this position is not maintainable for the following reasons:—

a) At the time of incorporation of the company, 50% of the shares were subscribed by its promoters, which are now being identified as sponsor share-holders, whilst the rest 50% of the shares were allotted through public subscription. Presently, 63% of the shares of the company are being traded through the stock exchange. It can be clearly seen that shares in the stock exchange contains sponsor shares and cannot be just treated as public shares.

b) If the company's argument is accepted, only share-holders holding sponsor directors, i.e. 28.84% of share-holders would vote in 70% of the directors of the company and this is against majority rule.

c) If 28.84% of share-holders vote in 70% of the directors of the company, the rest 22% of the share-holders who are entitled to vote in sponsor directors would be disenfranchised.

d) Moreover, as the 63% share-holders are trading through CDBL cannot identify themselves as holding either sponsor shares or public shares, they will be disenfranchised from voting in the AGM.

20. Mr Imam, the learned Counsel also submitted that the 3,00,000 shares that have been issued by the respondent No. 1 company are all ordinary shares with no special rights and privileges attached to any particular class of shares; accordingly all share-holders enjoy equal rights in respect of voting and dividends which are the principle rights that shares carry.

21. Mr Imam also submitted that since all issued shares were of one class i.e. ordinary shares ranking pari passu i.e. with equal rights in all respects, these rights will continue even after dematerialization, which does not in any manner alter the rights attached to the shares particularly because of the merger of the identity of the sponsor and public shares of the elimination of any/all distinction between them in the CDS system CDBL has no means of maintaining such distinction even on re-materialization into script from. He submitted that section 76 of the Insurance Act, 2010 read with SEC Notification No. SEC/CMRRCD/ 2006-158/ Admin/02-064th January, 2006 in respect of election of 2 independent directors effectively means 28.84% sponsor shares elect 14 out of 20 directors of the respondent company. According to Mr Imam the consequence of disfranchising the majority share-holders from electing the majority of the directors (i.e. 14 out of 20) would destroy one of the most fundamental concepts of company law i.e. majority rule as enunciated in the classic case of Foss vs Harbottle (1843) 2 Hare 461.

22. Mr Imam submitted that prospectus governing the issue of public shares does not limit their rights, unlike other share-holders, to elect only public directors. He submitted that section 91 read with the compulsory regulations of the Companies Act, 1994 guarantees the rights of the ordinary share-holders in electing the directors of the company. Section 76 of the Insurance Act, 2010 does not deal with voting rights to elect directors and Rule 15B of the said Rules is inapplicable and/or overridden by the CDBL system having a non-obstante clause in the governing law i.e. The Depository Act, 1999 and the Depository Regulations, 2003.

23. Regarding "Record Date" Mr Imam, the learned counsel submitted that it has been argued by the Vice Chairman of the company that SEC Notification dated 26-11-2001 will be applicable in setting the record date of the company for the 24th ACM. Such an argument was placed before this Court earlier in ABM Khaliquzzaman vs United Commercial Bank reported in 28 BLD (HCD) 635. The above judgment of this Court has been upheld by the Appellate Division by Civil Appeal Nos. 319-321 of 2008. Further, following the above judgment, SEC published Notification Nos. SEC /CMRRCD/ 2008-183/ Admin/ 03-36 dated 05 October 2009 and Notification No. SEC/CMRRCD/ 2009-193/ Part II/ 35/ Admin/ 03-43 dated 4 May 2010 setting the record date.

24. Mr Imam further submitted that record date is the date declared by an insurer for identifying the owners of a certain class of securities listed in the Depository Register for the owners to be identifiable for participation in general meeting, extra ordinary general meeting etc to cast vote as for transfer of transmitting dividends, interests, proxies, financial reports, and other documentation to them. Dhaka Stock Exchange by its Notification dated 18-3-2010 (published on 31-03-2010) amended the provisions of the Regulation 36(a)(4) of the listing Regulation of DSE and defined record date in the following terms:—

"the words "book closing date" and 'book closer date' shall be replaced by the words, 'book closer date' or 'record date' as the case may be."

25. Thereafter, the SEC has defined record date in its latest Notification No. SEC/ CMRRCD/ 2009-193/ part-II/ 35/ Admin/ 03-43 dated 4-5-2010 which provides as follows:—

a) The record date or commencement of book closure period of the listed security issuers shall be as per requirements in the listing regulations of the stock exchanges.

b) Annual General Meeting (AGM) shall be held by the listed security issuers within 45 (forty five) working days from the record date or completion of book closure period, as the case may be.

26. Mr Imam, the learned counsel submitted that this Court has power to fix a new record date in accordance with the above provisions of law. It is to be noted that both the company and the chairman of the company in this affidavit-in-oppositions have conceded to this position that the Court has power to fix a new record date for the pending AGMs.

27. In respect of an "Independent Election Commission", Mr Imam submitted that respondent No. 1 company is involved in a number of litigations namely, Writ Petition No. 6029 of 2005, Writ Petition No. 4673 of 2006 and Writ Petition No. 4733 of 2007, currently pending before the Hon'ble High Court Division. These litigations arise out of years of mistrust between the directors and the shareholders of the Company. Mr Imam has given description of the aforesaid litigations in the following manner:—

1. Writ Petition No. 6029 of 2005 was filed by one Md Serajul Munir, a policy-holder of life insurance policy of the respondent No. 1 Company, challenging election of policy holder-directors held in the meeting on 31-7-2005 on the basis that the election process was vitiated with illegality and mal-practice. This court after hearing the petitioner issued a Rule Nisi on 21-8-2005 calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the election of twelve life policy holder directors held on 31-07-2005 should not be declared to be illegal, without lawful authority and of no legal effect.

2. Writ Petition No. 4673 of 2006 was filed by the present respondent No. 2A impugning the failure of the Chief Controller of Insurance to investigate into the affairs of the respondent No. 1 company and to pass necessary orders and directions in the public interest and to ensure protection of interest of holders of insurance policies and to ensure proper management of the respondent No. 1 company. This Court issued a Rule Nisi on 27-3-2007 upon the Chief Controller of Insurance as to why the impugned action as detailed in the writ petition showing continuous failure of the Chief Controller of Insurance in discharging his function should not be declared to be not in accordance with law.

3. Writ Petition No. 4733 of 2007 was filed by the respondent No. 1 company, Delta Life Insurance Company Limited, impugning the recommendation issued by the Chief Controller of Insurance of appointment of Administrator for the respondent No. 1 company pursuant to the provisions of section 52A(1) of the then Insurance Act, 1938. The Chief Controller of Insurance had made such recommendations for, inter alia, the failure on the part of the respondent No. 1 company to hold its annual general meetings, dispute between sponsor and public directors which was resulting in the failure on the part of the management of the company to control the company pursuant to the requirements of the Insurance Act, the Insurance Rules and the Companies Act and inability of the policy holder directors to participate in the company meetings. This Court after hearing the petitioner issued Rule Nisi on 4-6-2007 upon the Chief Controller of Insurance and the Secretary, Ministry of Commerce to show cause as to why they should not be directed to take any steps for appointment of any Administrator in the respondent No. 1 company till disposal of the report submitted pursuant to the order dated 27-3-2007 passed in Writ Petition No. 4673 of 2006.

28. Mr Imam, the learned counsel by referring to the above litigations, submitted that although the above litigations do not bar the respondent no. 1 company from holding its AGMs, keeping in view the mistrust between the directors and the share-holders of the Company, this Court ought to pass necessary orders for appointment of a neutral and independent Election Commission comprising of 3 or 5 members, who are not associated with the respondent No. 1 company in any manner, for conducting a free and fair neutral election of directors in the pending six AGMs of the company.

29. Mr Ahsanul Karim, the learned Counsel appearing with Mr Khairul Alam Choudhury, learned counsel for respondent No. 2A in Matter No. 61 of 2010 and petitioner in Matter No. 61 of 2011 is not maintainable because condonation of delay has been sought for financial years ending on 2004-2008 whereas under section 81 of the Companies Act the condonation of delay must be for calendar years. In this regard Mr Karim, the learned Counsel read out section 3(19) of the General Clauses Act, 1897 which provides that 'financial year" shall mean the year commencing on the first day of July ending on the 30th day of June. He submitted that unless the prayer is amended this Court cannot grant substantive relief to the petitioner in Matter No. 61 of 2010.
