54. Shares inherently carry certain rights. These are called ordinary shares. The allottee and subsequent transferee shall equally enjoy the rights inherently attached to the shares. Paragraph 6.009 of Palmer's Company Law (Sweet & Maxwell's Loose leaf filing Guide Palmer Release 125: April 2010) articulates some of the rights which a share inherently carries. The said paragraph 6.009 of the Palmer's Company Law reads as follows:—

"6.009. The principal rights which a share may carry are derived from the statutory contract of the articles constituted by section 33. These are:—

(1) the right to a dividend if, while the company is a going concern, a dividend is duly declared; vs.

(2) the right to vote either at meetings and on written resolutions of members, as appropriate; or

(3) the right, in a winding up of the company, to participate in the distribution of the assets of the company after the payment of debts."

55. However, often the companies limited by shares issue shares with some extra ordinary rights, obligations or restrictions attaching thereto and thus makes classification of shares by way of attaching different rights or obligations to different classes of shares. In this respect paragraph 6.016 of Palmer's Company Law (Sweet & Maxwell's Loose leaf Filing Guide: Palmer Release 125: April 2010) read that:

"6.016: there is a presumption that the rights attaching to shares rank pari passu so that the holders participate equally in the benefits of membership. But this presumption is displaced when different shares carry different rights. Those shares then constitute different classes of shares. [-------].

56. Classification of shares by way of attaching different rights thereto is recognized in our jurisdiction as well. This is why section 71 of the Companies Act, 1994 provides protection of variation of rights attached to different classes of shares. From meticulous reading of section 71 of the Companies Act, 1994, I am fully convinced that classification of shares is allowed to be created by way of attaching different rights, obligations or restrictions to the shares. Section 71(1) of Companies Act, 1994 states as follows:—

“ ৭১. বিশেষ শ্রেনীর শেয়ার হোল্ডারগনের অধিকার(১)বিভিন্ন শ্রেনীর শেয়ার বিভক্ত শেয়ার মূলধন-বিশিষ্ট কোন কোম্পানীর সংঘস্মারকে বা সংঘবিধিতে যদি এইরুপ বিধান থাকে যে, কোন শ্রেনীর ইস্যুকৃত শেয়ারের ধারকগনের একটি নিদিষ্ট আনুপাতিক সদস্যের সম্মতি সাপেক্ষে অথবা তাহাদের একটি পৃথক সভায় গৃহীত সিদ্দান্ত সাপেক্ষে, উক্ত শ্রেনীর শেয়ারের সহিত সংশ্লিষ্ট অধিকারের পরিবর্তন করা যাইবে, এবং যদি তদানুসারে উক্ত শ্রেনীর শেয়ারের সহিত সংশ্লিষ্ট অধিকার পরিবর্তন করা হয়, তাহা হইলে উক্ত শ্রেনীর ইস্যুকৃত মোট শেয়ারের অন্যুন শতকরা দশ ভাগ শেয়ারের ধারকগন, যাহার সম্মতি দান করেন নাই বা পরিবর্তনের সিদ্ধান্তের পক্ষে ভোট দান করেন নাই তাহারা, উক্ত পরিবর্তন বাতিলের জন্য আদালতে আবেদন করিতে পারিবেন এবং এইরুপ কোন আবেদন করা হইলে আদালত কর্তৃক অনুমোদিত না হওয়া পর্যন্ত উক্ত পরিবর্তন কার্যকর হইবে না।

57. 1 am also convinced from the plain reading of the provision of section 71 of the Companies Act, 1994 that the legislature under the said section 71 has given protection to the rights attached to the shares উক্ত শ্রেনীর শেয়ারের সহিত সংশ্লিষ্ট অধিকার which manifests that such rights attached thereto run with the shares. In other words if such class of shares are transferred then such rights are also transferred along with the shares and subsequent transferee shall enjoy the said rights. These rights are covenant in rem, because such rights will not be extinguished by way of transfer of the shares.

58. When a different right is attached to a class of shares, then the said shares are referred to as "preference shares". Gower on Principles of Modern Company Law (Eighth Edition 2008: First South Asian Edition 2008 at page 822, paragraph 2) described preferential shares as hereunder:—

"The truth of the matter is that an enormous variety of different rights, relating to dividends, return of capital, voting, conversion into ordinary shares, redemption and other matters, may be attached to classes of shares, all of which are conventionally described as "preference" shares. [--------].

59. Such preferential rights are attached to shares. So such rights, which stem form the preferential shares, are convenient in rem that runs with the shares and change of holder of such shares does not vary the force of such right attached to such class of shares.

60. Now, whether any particular share is ordinary shares or preferential share or any other class of share depend upon the construction of the Articles of Association of the company or other instrument for issuing or creating such shares. For this purpose Court can have recourse to various "cannons of construction" of documents for interpreting the same. I have perused the Articles of Association of the respondent No. 1 company and other documents annexed in the both matters. Articles 6, 49 and 54 of the Articles of Association of the respondent No. 1 company empowers the respondent No. 1 company to attach any special right or privilege to any share and creation of preferential share and variation of rights attached to different classes of shares. Article 6 of the Articles of Association of the respondent No. 1 company reads as follows:—

"6. Subject to any special rights or privileges for the time being attached to any issued shares, the new share shall be issued upon such terms and conditions and with such rights and privileges annexed thereto as the resolution creating them shall direct, and if no direction be given, as the Directors shall determine and in particular such shares may be issued with a preferential or qualified right to dividends and in distribution of assets of the Company and with a special or without any right of voting."

61. This Article 6 of Articles of Association of the respondent No. 1 company protects existing preferential shares and other classes of shares with any right or privilege attached thereto and this Article 6 also empowers the respondent No. 1 company to issue/allot new preferential shares or various classes of shares with various rights and privileges. This Article 6 does not ipso facto create any preferential share or classes of shares. On perusal of the Articles of Association and other documents annexed by both petitioners and other parties. I have not found any provision in the Articles of Association creating any preferential share or classes of shares attaching different rights thereto. Neither I have come across any other documents creating any preferential shares or classes of shares in the respondent No. 1 company. All the shares held by the promoters/ sponsor share-holders of the company and the public through IPO are ordinary shares having equal rights and privileges, or obligations attached thereto. In view of the matter, through I find force in the submission of Mr Karim that any right attached to shares does not extinguish in the event the script shares are converted into dematerialized shares through Central depository System, but I find it redundant and academic to address in the instant case to the issue whether categorizations/ classifications of shares are blurred in the event the script shares are converted into dematerialized form through Central Depository System and whether Central Depository Bangladesh Limited (CDBL) has failed to manage a system to identify the different classes of shares in dematerialized form, since in the instant case the respondent No. 1 Company has not issued different classes of shares or preferential shares. This issue should remain open for resolution in proper case in future. Therefore, the submission of Dr Zahir and Mr Imam, the learned Counsels for the petitioner regarding difficulties in identifying classes of shares in dematerialized form are not relevant for disposal of the present matters. Hence I hold that all the shares so far issued by the respondent No. 1 company are ordinary shares.

62. As opposed to attaching rights to shares, often Articles of Association of the company or other instruments such as special resolution of the company attach special rights expressly or by necessary implication, to a particular person or set of persons. Such person or persons enjoy the rights attached to them so long they remain in the company and such right does not run with the shares. For instance, a particular share-holder is named in the Articles of Association to remain life long Chairman or Managing Director or Auditor etc.; or Articles of Association provides or special resolution or agreement provides that unless a particular share-holder or a particular number of share-holders from a defined set of share-holders appears in the meeting, there will not be any quorum for meeting; or Article of Association or other instruments creates a right that existing share-holders or particular named share-holder/ share-holders shall be offered first in the event of allotment of new shares or in the event of transfer of shares by other share-holders i.e. a pre-emptive right, or a right to right to refuse first is created. Even section 155 of the Companies Act, 1994 creates a pre-emptive right for offering the existing share-holders first in pro rata in the event of allotment of new shares to the existing share-holders. These are examples of rights attach to share-holders. These rights are not attached to the shares. So such rights do not run with the shares. In other words, the subsequent transferee of shares does not acquire such rights of the transferor who would earlier enjoy such rights. Such rights are covenant in personam. If the share-holder enjoying such special rights transfers his shares, then the ultimate transferee shall not able to enjoy the said rights. By way of attaching different rights to the share-holders, different class of share-holders are created. In our jurisdiction such classification of share-holders are also recognized, which gets legal footing from section 85(1)(e) of the Companies Act, 1994. Section 85(1)(e) states that share-holders shall enjoy the same rights and be subject to the same liabilities as all other share-holders of the same class. Section 85(1)(e) of the Companies Act, 1994 allows different classes of share-holders and amongst the own class the share-holders will enjoy same rights and be subjected to same obligations. Such classes of share-holders are created expressly or by necessary implication. Whether there is different classes of share-holders depends upon construction of constitutive document of the company i.e. the Articles of Association or any other instrument creating such classification of share-holders by way of attaching different set of share-holders. For this purpose as well the Court can take recourse to various "cannons of construction" of documents for ascertaining whether there are classes of share-holders with different rights attached to them. Applicable laws may also expressly or by necessary implication, create different classes of share-holders having different rights attached to them. Now I shall consider whether the Articles of Association of the respondent No. 1 company and provisions of laws of the land applicable thereto or any other instrument, either expressly or by necessary implication, has created different classes of share-holders with different rights attached to them.

63. I have perused Article 5(b) of the Articles of Association of the respondent No. 1 company Articles 5(b) reads as follows:—

"5(b) The initial paid-up capital of the Company shall not be below Taka 3,00,00,000 (Taka three crore) of which 50% shall be subscribed by the promoters and the remaining 50% shall be offered for public subscription within a period of 3 years from the date of incorporation of the Company. The portion of the public issue of shares of Taka 1,50,00,000 (One Crore Fifty Lacs) remaining unsubscribed shall be underwritten by the scheduled banks and financial institutions."

64. Article 5(b) categorically make two classes of share-holders,one is public share-holders/ public subscribers and another is promoters i.e., sponsor share-holders/ sponsor subscribers. Further, I have perused Article 89 and Article 89(A) of the Articles of Association, which stages as follows:—

"89. Save as provided in Article 102(A) the qualification of a Director shall be holding in his own name and right along and not jointly with any other person, shares of the nominal value of Taka 2,00,000 (Taka two lac), relaxable in the case of Directors in the case of Directors representing interest holding shares of the requisite value.

89(A). Directors from amongst the policyholders be elected for a period of three years as per section 48(1) of Insurance Act, 1938 and such Policyholder Directors shall not be required to hold any qualification shares.

Provided that the qualification of a director from public subscribers shall be his holding minimum shares to the face value of Taka 10,000 (Taka ten thousand) statutory bodies, trust and such like that he/ she represents, at least six months before the date of election and that he/ she is not disqualified as per provisions of the Insurance Act or Rules or any other laws of the country."

65. This Articles 89 and 89(A) of the Articles of Association crystal clearly shows that there are two classes of share-holders namely sponsor share-holders and public share-holders/public subscribers. The public subscribers have right to be elected as director only having qualifying shares to the face of Taka 10,000 and whereas the sponsor share-holders can be elected as directors when they have minimum qualifying shares of nominal value of Taka 2,00,000. Further, under the Article 5(b) of the Articles of Association the sponsor share-holders collectively has right to hold 50% of the paid up capital whereas the public subscribers as well has collective right to hold 50% of the paid up capital. All these rights are attached to the share-holders in personam. If the sponsor share-holders/promoters transfer their certain number of shares to any public then the said shares does not carry these rights to the public subscribers. This classification of share-holders is also recognized in the Insurance Act, 2010 also recognizes the classification of the share-holders. Clause (Ka) of Schedule 1 of the Insurance Act, 2010 provides that the sponsor share-holders/ promoters (উদ্যোক্তাগন) must subscribe 60% to the paid up capital and the rest 40% shall be open to be subscribed by the public subscribers. This provision of the Insurance Act, 2010 is not applicable to the companies starting business under the repealed Insurance Act, 1938. At the relevant time of incorporation of the respondent No. 1 company, Clause 1(a) of the 7th Schedule of the repealed Insurance Act, 1938 as well provided that the sponsors must subscribe 50% to the paid up capital. So I have no hesitation to arrive to the finding that, though the respondent No. 1 company does not have classification of shares, but the respondent No. 1 company does have two classes of share-holders, namely sponsor share-holders and public share-holders. The name of "promoters" or sponsor subscribers are interchangeably used for the name "sponsor share-holders", whereas the name "public subscribers" are also interchangeably used for the name "public share-holders". But Articles of Association of the respondent No. 1 company do not define the periphery of the word "sponsor share-holders/ promoters". Neither the Companies Act, nor the laws of Securities defines the ambit of sponsor share-holders. In English Jurisdiction as well the word "promoter/ sponsor" is not defined. In modern corporate age, the word "promoter/ sponsor share-holders" acquires its meaning and colour from the relevant fact and circumstances. In this respect Gower on Principles of Modern Company Law (Eighth Edition 2008: First South Asian Edition 2008 at page 106 paragraph 3) couched the practical difficulties, when the periphery of promoters is required to be clarified, in the following words:—

"Who constitutes a promoter in any particular case is therefore a question of fact. The expression has never been clearly defined either judicially or legislatively, despite the fact that it is frequently used both in decisions and statutes. So far as the promoter is concerned this imposes no particular hardship; as we shall see, the relevant duty is merely to act with good faith towards the company and this should occur, whether legally compelled or not. But from the point of view of the company the vagueness of the term is apt to be embarrassing when legislation requires promoters to be named or transactions with them to be disclosed."

66. Though, it is difficult to give a legal definition of "promoters/ sponsor share-holders" as a general principle of law applicable to all instance irrespective of differential facts and circumstances, but it is not practically impossible for the respondent No. 1 company to ascertain as to who are "promoters/ sponsor share-holders" in the instant case. As I have already found that there are two groups of share-holders namely sponsor share-holders and public subscribers. So sponsor share-holders are those members of the company who are not public subscribers. The relevant Insurance Act required that 50% of the shares to be subscribed by the public and 50% of shares to be subscribed by the sponsors. So those who become member of the respondent No. 1 company by way of subscribing the said 50% shares reserved for the public are public subscribers and rest of the members of the company are sponsor share-holders. Section 3(2) of the Capital Issues (Continuance of Control) Act, 1947 (as then was in force) required that a company must obtain consent of the Government for making any public offer of securities. Further section 4 of the said Capital Issues (Continuance of Control) Act, 1947 (as then was in force) also required the respondent No. 1 company to issue prospectus offering for subscription or publicly offering for sale securities stating that it has obtained consent of the Government. Under the provision of said Capital Issues (Continuance of Control) Act, 1947 (as then was in force), the Government vide Memo No. MF/ Inv-42/86/508 dated 02-11-1986 accorded its consent to public offer to the extent of 50% shares of the respondent No. 1 company. Relevant part of the said consent of Government dated 1-11-1986 runs as follows:—

"With reference to The Law Centre's letter No. TLC/ 2034/86 dated 25-10-1986, this is to say that, subject to the conditions stated in enclosed sheets (pages 1 to 3), consent is hereby given under the Capital issues (Continuance of Control) Act, 1947 to the proposed issue of share Capital in Bangladesh by the above Public Limited Company proposed to be registered in Bangladesh to the value of Taka 3,00,000 (Taka three crore) only divided into 3,00,000 ordinary shares of Taka 100 each to be issued at par for cash in the following manner.

(a)	Sponsors/ Directors (50%)  1,50,000 shares of Taka 100 each; and

(b)	General Public (50%) Taka 1,50,000 shares of Taka 10.00 each"

67. Thereafter, the respondent No. 1 company in the year 1995 allocated the said 50% shares reserved for public through IPO under the relevant laws and regulations of Securities and Exchange Commission. Therefrom, the public at large got their entrance into the company by way of subscribing shares through IPO and became members of the respondent No. 1 company as public subscribers. It is a very normal case and practicably possible by the respondent No. 1 company to ascertain who became members of the respondent No. 1 company by way of subscribing shares reserved for the public through IPO. Therefore, once it can be ascertained who are public subscribers (by way of subscribing reserve 50% shares for public through IPO), the rest of the members of the company whose name appears in the company are sponsor share-holders or promoters. Therefore, with certainty the members of the respondent No. 1 company whose name appears in the Articles of Association (only those who are still existing as members) and also those who become member of the respondent No. 1 company by way of allotment of shares by the respondent No. 1 company directly immediately before IPO are no doubt sponsor share-holders/ promoters in the instant case. Therefore, I find that in any event, for the purpose of the instant case, those who became member of the respondent No. 1 company thorough IPO by way of subscribing shares reserved for public and subsequently through further public offerings in future are and will be public subscribers and also those who are for the first time inducted into the company as member by way of purchasing shares through stock markets, be it from sponsor share-holders or public subscribers, or those who are for the first time inducted into the company as member by way of otherwise acquiring shares from another public subscribers in any manner are "public subscribers" and the rest of the members of the respondent No. 1 company are sponsor share-holders.

68. Now the moot question is whether these two classes of share-holders i.e. sponsor share-holders and public subscribers, do have different right in respect of electing directors of the respondent No. 1 company attached to them and if any, then whether such right is valid in the eye of law.

69. I have considered the provisions of section 76 of the Insurance Act, 2010 very meticulously. Section 76 fixed a ceiling for the size of Board of Directors of the Insurance Company to the maximum number of and also fixed the maximum number of directors from the aforesaid two classes of share-holders. This section provides that not more than 12 directors can be elected from amongst the sponsor share-holders, whereas 6 directors can be elected from amongst the public subscribers. For sake of convenience section 76 is reproduced hereunder:—

“ ৭৬। বীমাকারীর পরিচালনা পর্যদ(১) বীমাকারী কোম্পানী আইন এর অধীনে নিবন্ধিত হইলে, উহার সংঘস্মারক বা সংঘবিধিতে যাহাই খাকুক না কেন উহার পরিচালকের সংখ্যা ২০ (বিশ) জনের অধিক হইবে না এবং সেইক্ষেত্রে ১২(বার) জন উদ্যোক্তা পরিচালক ও ৬(ছয়) জন জনগনের অংশের শেয়ারগ্রহীতা পরিচালনা এবং ২(দুই) জন নিরপেক্ষ (independent) পরিচালক থাকিবেন। (২) শেয়ারগ্রহীতাগন বিধি দ্বারা নির্ধারিত পদ্দতিতে পরিচালক নির্বাচন করিবে।”

<u>70. Section 76(1) gives right to the share-holders. This right is not attached to shares. The promoters have right to elect 12 directors in the board. Promoters are those who have originally subscribed to the memorandum and Articles of Association. So promoters or sponsors are the original share-holders, who floated the company by way of subscribing to the memorandum and Articles of Association named therein. If the promoters transfer their shares then the transferee does not become promoters or sponsor share-holders. This right is a right in personam. This right can be enjoyed by the promoters so long they remain as member of the company. Section 76(2) provides that share-holders shall elect directors in the manner prescribed by the rules framed under the Insurance Act, 2010. The Insurance Rules, 1958 is deemed to be the Rules framed under the Insurance Act, 2010. I shall discuss the manner prescribed by Rules, 1958 later. Before that, I shall consult the Articles of Association of the company attaching any right, if any, to the said two classes of share-holders namely sponsor share-holder and public subscribers in respect of electing sponsor directors and public directors respectively.</u>

71. I have also considered Articles 95, 96 and 97 of the Articles of Association of the respondent No. 1 company. Article 95, 96 reads as follows:—

"95. Subject to the Article No. 102 & 103 at the first ordinary meeting of the company, the whole of the Directors shall retire from office and at the ordinary Meeting in every subsequent year, one third of the Directors representing sponsor share-holders inclusive of co-opted directors for the time being and one third of the Directors from public subscribers, if their number is not three or a multiple of three, then the number nearest to one-third, shall retire from office. The Directors from amongst the policyholders shall not be liable to retire by rotation.

96. The Directors to retire in every year shall be those who have longest in office since their last election, but as between persons who become Directors on the same day those to retire shall (unless they otherwise agree among themselves) be determined by lot. A retiring director shall be eligible for re-election.

Provided that retiring sponsor directors shall be re-elected by the sponsor share-holder while retiring directors from public subscribers shall be re-elected by the public subscribers:

97. The Company at the General Meeting at which a Director retires in manner aforesaid may fill up the vacated  office by electing a person thereto."

72. Article 95 of the Articles of Association requires retirement of one-third directors representing sponsor share-holders and also one-third directors from public subscribers to retire in very ordinary meeting of the calendar year. However, retiring directors from both classes of share-holders have right to be re-elected. But only the sponsor share-holders shall have right to re-elect only the directors representing sponsor share-holders, whereas the public subscribers shall have right to re-elect only the directors representing the public subscribers. This manner of re-elected directors attaching rights to respective classes of share-holders has been provided in the proviso to Article 96 of Association. Now the question is how a share-holder can be inducted in the board as a fresh director. Article 97 of the Articles of Association provides that a person can be elected as a director to fill up the vacated office of a retiring directors and such a person can be elected as a director "in the manner aforesaid" under the said Article 97 refers to the manner of election prescribed in the preceding Article No. 96. Therefore, the construction of the Articles of Association transpires to me that in view of Article 97 read with Article 96 sponsor share-holders shall elect the sponsor directors (উদ্যোক্তা পরিচালক) and the public subscribers shall elect public directors for the purpose of constituting board under section 76(1) of the Insurance Act, 2010. Therefore, Articles of Association has given special rights attached to the sponsor share-holders to elect directors representing sponsor share-holders and has also given special rights attached to the public share-holders to elect directors representing public subscribers. These rights attached to sponsor share-holders and public subscribers respectively are right in personam. This right does not run with the shares.

73. Section 76(2) of the Insurance Act, 2010 provides that directors shall be elected in the manner prescribed in the Rules. The Insurance Rules, 1958 is deemed to be Rules framed under the Insurance Act, 2010 in view of section 160(2)(q) of the Insurance Act, 2010. Rule 15A and Rule 15B of the Insurance Rules, 1958 provides the manner for election of directors by public subscribers. The Insurance Rules, 1958 does not provide any thing for electing directors representing sponsor share-holders. Rule 15B(1) of the Insurance Rules, 1958 confines the public subscribers to elect the directors representing public subscribers. Rule 15B(1) of the Insurance Rules, 1958 states as follows:—

"15B(1) The holders of public holders of public subscription shares shall elect the Directors under rule 15A."

74. Dr Zahir, the learned Counsel argued that in view of Rule 15B(1) of the Insurance Rules, 1958 public subscribers shall elect directors representing public subscribers as well as the directors representing sponsor share-holder, but sponsor share-holders shall not be eligible to elect directors representing public subscribers. I find it difficult to agree with the submissions made by Dr Zahir Rules 15B(1) does not speak that public subscribers shall also elect directors representing sponsor share-holders. Rule 15B(1) simply provides that public subscribers shall elect directors representing public subscribers. This means that the right of public subscribers to elect directors is confined to the election of directors representing the public subscribers. So the public subscribers cannot exercise their right of election beyond directors representing public subscribers i.e. they cannot elect directors representing sponsor share-holders. Rule 15B(1) not only exclude all other share-holders (i.e. sponsor share-holders) other than public subscribers to elect director representing public subscribers, but the said Rule 15B(1) in the same vein is restrictive clause upon public subscribers in electing directors representing public subscribers only. If the legislature had the intention only to debar the sponsor share-holders in participating election of directors representing public subscribers then the legislature would provide in the plain language to that effect stating that in clear language that the sponsor share-holders shall not be eligible to participate in electing directors representing public subscribers. So I am fully convinced that Rule 15B(1) completely attached rights to public subscribers to elect only directors representing public subscribers and also by necessary implication debars the public subscribers to participate in electing sponsor directors and also debars sponsor share-holders in electing public directors.

75. The express mention of "directors under the Rule 15A" (i.e. public subscribers) in Rule 15B(1) by necessary implication excludes all other share-holders other than public subscribers. So right of public subscribers is delimited in electing the directors under the Rule 15A only i.e. only the directors representing public subscribers. It is an old maxim the expression unius exclusion alterious, which means that express mention of one or more thing of particular class is regarded as silently excluding all other member of the class. In this respect Maxwell on the Interpretation of Statutes (12 Edition 1969 at page 293) reads as follows:—

"Expressio unius exclusion exclusion alterius.

By the rule usually known in the form of this Latin maxim, mention of one or more things of a particular class may be regarded as silently excluding all other members of the class: expressum facit cessare tacitum. Further, where a statute uses two words or expressions, one of which generally includes the other, the more general term is taken in a sense excluding the less general one: otherwise there would have been little point in using the latter as well as the former."

76. Therefore, in view of the above matter, I find that public subscribers shall elect directors under Rule 15A, means that public subscribers shall not elect other directors other than directors under Rule 15A i.e. public subscribers. So I do not find any force in the submission of Dr Zahir that public subscribers shall elect the sponsor directors as well.

77. Dr Zahir, the learned Senior Counsel for the petitioner further argued that the proviso to Article 96 confining right of sponsor shares to elect sponsor directors and right of public subscribers to elect public directors is ultra vires the Companies Act, 1994. Dr Zahir argued that Article 96 of Articles of Association is contrary to section 91(1)(b) of the Companies Act, 1994 as well as Regulations 80, 81 and 61 of the Schedule-1 to the Companies Act, 1994. I do not find Article 96 contrary to the Companies Act, 1994. Section 91(1)(b) of the Companies Act states that:—

“ ৯১(১) কোম্পানীর সংঘবিধিতে যাহা কিছুই থাকুক না কেন-

(খ) কোম্পানীর পরিচালকগন উহার সাধারন সভায় কোম্পানীর সদস্যগন কর্তৃক তাহাদের মধ্য হইতে নির্বাচিত হইবেন”

78. Section 91(1)(b) of the Companies Act, 1994 does not offend the provision of Article 96 of the Articles of Association. In fact section 91(1)(b) of the Companies Act, 1994 imposed certain mandatory requirements in respect of election of directors of the company. The mandatory conditions as required under section 91(1)(b) of the Companies Act, 1994 to be followed for pursuing election of directors are following:—

"Director of the company to be eligible for being elected as director, he himself must be a member of the company.

i.	The voters to be eligible to elect a director must be member of the company and none but member of the company can be eligible voter for electing director.

ii.	Election of a director must be held in the general meeting as opposed to any other meeting such as board meeting."

79. No Article of the Articles of Association of the respondent No. 1 company or Article 96 makes any provision that any person other than member of the company can be eligible to contest election for the office of directors; or that any person who is not member of the company can vote for electing a director of the company; or that election of the director can be held in the meeting of board or any other meeting except general meeting. Therefore, none of the provisions of the Articles of Association offends section 91(1)(b) of the Companies Act, 1994. Article 96 only provides that directors representing sponsor directors shall be elected by sponsor-director and director representing public subscribers shall be elected by public subscribers and by way of providing two groups of share-holders, Article 96 does not conflict section 91(1)(b) of the Companies Act, 1994 rather Article 96 is fully in conformity with section 91(1)(b) of the Companies Act, 1994 since during election in compliance of Article 96 a director must be a member of the company; a voter must also be a member of director, and election of director will be held in general meeting. In other way around section 91(1)(b) of the Companies Act, 1994 does not restrict or prohibit making two groups of share-holders, one group having no right to elect directors from other group and the same is mutually applicable in both groups. Further, Dr Zahir argued that each share shall have one vote and, as such, Article 96 offends Regulations 61, 81 and 81. I have found that Regulation 61 is not mandatory regulation. In any event Article 96 does not confront the principle one share shall have one vote, since once allowed to cast vote each share shall carry the weight one vote, and shares of none of the eligible voter in the respective group shall carry the weight of more than one vote. Further Regulations 80 and 81 relates to retirement by rotation and re-election. The Articles of Association of the company keeps provision of retirement by rotation. So none of the provision of the Articles of Association negates the effect of Regulations 80 and 81. Thus, I have not found any provision in the Companies Act, 194 which restricts or prohibits classification of share-holders into different classes. Different classes of share-holders are created by attaching separate rights or special rights to the different classes of share-holders. Rather I have found that Companies Act, 1994 inspires creation of classes amongst the share-holders and enforces enjoyment of same rights amongst the same group. Section 85(1)ঙ) of the Companies Act, 1994 can be reproduced here for better understanding from this perspective. Section 85(1)(ঙ) of the Companies Act, 1994 reads as follows:—

“ ৮৫(১)(ঙ) কোন শেয়ার হোল্ডার, যাহার নাম কোম্পানীর শেয়ার হোল্ডারদের বহিত লিপিবদ্ধ করা হইয়াছে তিনি, একই শ্রেনীর অন্যান্য শেয়ার হোল্ডার যে রুপ অধিকার ভোগ এবং দায় দায়িত্ব বহন করিবেন, তদরুপ একই অধিকার ভোগ এবং দায়-দায়িত্ব বহন করিবেন।”

80. So it appears that the literal interpretation of section 85(1)(s) of the Companies Act, 1994 in a very simple language transpires that share-holder of same class shall enjoy same rights. So one share-holder or a particular class cannot raise objection that share-holder of different group are enjoying different rights, neither one share-holder of particular class can wield a right of another class of share-holders. Therefore, if attachment of different rights to different classes of shares are treated as ultra virus the Companies Act, 1994, as argued by Dr Zahir, the whole sanction of the provision under section 85(1)(ঙ) of the Companies Act, shall be frustrated, futile and negated.

81. In this respect as I have already observed in the preceding paragraph, I find very strong persuasive value from a decision of House of Lords in the case of Bushell vs Faith reported in [1970] WLR 272, which expounded that a provision of Articles of Association cannot be ultra vires the Companies Act, if the legislature does not restrict or prohibit in clear language the action under the provision of the Articles of Association. In the said case of Bushel! vs Faith, in the company in question there were three share-holders, namely Mrs Anna Bushell, Mrs Geoffrey Leopold Faith & Dr Kathleen Bayne, having 100 Shares each. Mrs Bushell and Dr Bayne being dissatisfied with the conduct of Mr Faith as director requisitioned of the general meeting of the company took consider and, if though fit, to pass a resolution for removal of the said Mr Faith from office as director. Under section 184(1) of the Companies Act, 1948 (statute of UK Parliament), a director can be removed by an ordinary resolution. Article 9 of the Articles of Association of the company in question provided that in the event of a resolution being proposed at any general meeting of the company for removal from office of any director, any shares held by that director intended to be removed shall on a pool in respect of such resolution carry the right to three votes per share. Mrs Bushell and Dr Bayne passed a resolution purportedly removing Mr Faith as director. Mrs Bushell and Dr Bayne contended that since simple resolution is required to remove a director under section 184(1), they have total 200 shares and Mr Faith has only 100 shares and, as such, Mr Faith has been lawfully removed by simple resolution. On the other hand, Mr Faith contended that under Article 9 in the event of removal his each shall carry 3 votes and, as such, total shares carry the weight of 300 votes and the shares of Mrs Bushell and Dr Bayne carry the weight of 200 votes and, as such, no resolution has been passed. In the said case, thereby moot question was whether Article 9 having defeated the sanction of 184(1) is void. The Court of Appeal held that the Companies Act, 1948 having not prohibited giving extra voting weight to a share, Article 9 is not ultra vires of section 148(1). The House of Lords by majority decision upheld the decision of Court of Appeal. Lord Upjohn in this regard articulated as follows:—

"parliament has never sought to fetter the right of the company to issue a share with such rights or restrictions as it may think fit. There is no fetter which compels the company to make the voting rights or restrictions of general application and it seems to me clear that such rights or restrictions can be attached to special circumstances and to particular types of resolution. This makes mockery of section 148; all that Parliament was seeking to do thereby was to make an ordinary resolution sufficient to remove a director. Had Parliament desired to go further and enact that every share entitled to vote should be deprived of its special rights under the articles it should have said so in plain terms by making the vote on a poll one vote one share. Then, what about shares, which had no voting, rights under the articles? Should not Parliament give them a vote when considering this completely artificial from of ordinary resolution? Suppose there had here been some preference shares in the name of Mr Faith's wife, which under the articles had in the circumstances no vote; why in justice should her voice be excluded from consideration in his artificial vote?"

82. In the instant case as well, I have not found any restriction or prohibition in the Companies Act, 1994 in classifying two groups of share-holders namely sponsor share-holders and public subscriber mutually debarring each group from participating in election of directors of other group. Articles of Association in proper construction having mutually curtailed right to vote of one group in electing directors from other group, any provision of law cannot be interpreted to give vote to the former group. Section 91(b) of the Companies Act, 1994 does not state that all the members/ share-holders of the company must have participation in the election of director, neither does section 91(1)(b) restrict or prohibit making two groups of share-holders one having no participation in electing directors from other group. If the legislature had otherwise intention, then the legislature in plain language would prohibit giving different rights of different groups of share-holders and section 85(1)(ঙ) would not encourage different rights amongst different groups of share-holders.

83. Decision of this Division in the case of Dr Monjurul Islam vs Al-Rajhi Hospital (Pvt) Ltd reported in 1 LG (2004) HCD 46 also expounded similar proposition of law. In the said case of Dr Monjurul Islam vs Al-Rajhi Hospital (Pvt) Ltd, Mr Justice ABM Khairul Haque (as his Lordship was then) held (Paragraph No. 30) as follows:—

"As such, the contention of Mr Rafiq-ul-Haque, Senior Advocate, that the provisions made in the articles of the company shall have no effect unless specifically provided in the Act itself is not correct, rather, the articles will be applicable unless it is inconsistent with any of the provisions of the act or is made inapplicable by a specific provision as in the case of sub-section 1 of section 85."

<u>84. The said case reported in 1 LG (2004) HCD 46 enunciated the proposition of law to the effect "any Act of Parliament or the Companies Act, 1994 or statutory instrument created thereunder" in sub silentio does invalidate a provision of the Articles of Association of the company or an action of the company. I have not found any provision of the Companies Act, 1994 or the Insurance Act, 2010 prohibiting or restricting classification of rights as to electing directing amongst the group of share-holders. Both Dr Zahir and Mr Akhter Imam argued that under section 76(2) the directors are to be elected in the manner as prescribed in the Rule and election of directors cannot be held as per Article 96 of the Articles of Association. I do not agree with the contentions made by Dr Zahir and Mr Akhter Imam. In the Insurance Rules there is no provision of election of directors of sponsor directors and, as such, this silent aspect of Insurance Rules does not invalidate the provisions of Articles of Association for electing directors as any of the provision of the Articles of Association is not inconsistent with Rule 15B of the Insurance Rules. Rather 15B in clear terms provides that the public subscribers shall elect public directors and they shall not elect a sponsor directors. Further, I find a logical conclusion can be drawn that it will be discriminatory if the public subscribers are allowed to elect sponsors directors when sponsors cannot elect public directors. The public subscribers are allowed to elect sponsor directors that will mean a preferential right given to public share-holders but the Articles of Association of the company has not given any such preferential right to any public subscribers on top of the sponsor share-holders. Therefore, I hold that Article 96 is fully consistent with Rule 15B of the side rules and sponsor share-holders shall elect sponsor directors and public subscribers shall elect public directors.</u>

85. As such I do not find any force in the argument of Dr Zahir, the learned counsel that proviso to Article 96 giving separate rights to two different classes, namely sponsor share-holders and public subscribes, allowing to elect directors of their respective class only is ultra vires the Companies Act, 1994 and Insurance Act, 2010.

86. I also do not find that the prospectus issued by the company operate as estoppel in respect of the issues specifically provided in Articles of Association. Documents which are deposited with a statutory or Government agency in compliance of law of the land, moreso if the public have access to the same, then the said document being in public domain are public documents. Articles of Association of a company is also a public document. Dr Zahir argued that prospectus provides that each share will have one voting right and since it does not prove that voting right will be limited to the effect that the holders of public shares will not be able to cast vote for election for sponsors-directors, the prospectus operates as estoppel upon the company to allow public subscriber to cast vote for election of sponsor-directors. This submission does not hold good since Articles of Association being a public document such omission in the prospectus to the effect as argued cannot operate as estoppel. Moreover, Articles of Association was part of the prospectus and therefore, the classification of share-holders with restriction as aforesaid was in disclosure procedure. So I find no substance in this submission. In this respect, Clause 20 of the Schedule 3 of the Companies Act, 1994 stipulates that the information as to restriction or privileges regarding voting of the members of the company must be stipulated in the prospectus. This Clause 20 manifestly shows that the Companies Act, 1994 recognizes classification of share-holders in terms of voting power. However, in failing to mentioning the same in the prospectus the provisions of the Companies Act, 1994 such as section 145 stipulates the consequences of civil liabilities and other. But the Companies Act, 1994 nowhere provide that for failing to mentioning the same, the terms of the Articles of Association of any company shall be invalidated. As such I find no substance in the argument of Dr Zahir failure to mentioning the classification of share-holders invalidate the right of the share-holders as to voting power.

87. Mr Imam, the learned counsel argued that a portion of the shares from both classes of share-holders have been converted into dematerialized form. As such he argued, from the face the shares it cannot be ascertained whether the holder of shares is a sponsor share-holder or a public subscribers and for this reason the public subscribers cannot be debarred from participating in the election of directors representing sponsor share-holders. I do not find any substance in this submission advanced by Mr Imam. Whether a person is a sponsor share-holder can be mentioned on the face of the Articles of Association, because the persons who subscribed to the Memorandum and Articles of Association as promoters are named in the Memorandum and Articles of Association. Therefore, the sponsor share-holders can easily be traced out on the face of the Articles of Association. From the list of share-holders obtained from CDBL as on the date of record date, it can easily be ascertained how many shares in dematerialized form are being held by a sponsor share-holders. Therefore, the total number of shares held by a particular share-holders, be sponsor share-holder or public subscribers, can be ascertained with sufficient certainty. On the other hand, as I have found above, there is no classes of shares in the respondent No. 1 company and, as such, whether categorization or identity of shares in dematerialized form is lost is immaterial. Therefore, I am not at all convinced with the submission of Mr Akhter Imam that as a result of shares 63% shares held by the share-holders by the company from the stock Exchange are not aware as to whether they are holding sponsor shares or public shares. I hold that the shares held by sponsors cannot be termed as 'sponsor share' since as I have already held that there is no special rights attached to shares, in other words all shares are ordinary shares and so long the sponsors will hold the same will be shares of sponsors and when the shares will be sold to public, the said shares will be shares of public subscribers. Therefore, after transferring the shares of sponsors to public the shares will no longer be sponsors' shares but the same will be of public shares. In this regard I find full force with the submission of Mr Karim, the learned counsel that promoters shall remain sponsor share-holders till they cease to have their membership of the company by way of transferring their entire shares. It further appears to me that the submission of the petitioner in Company Matter No. 61 of 2010 is contradictory of prayer made by him. If there is no classification of share-holders with separate voting rights then the petitioner would not have asked for votes in two ballots. However, the company may trace and identify sponsor shares amongst of dematerialized shares of the company as per law and rules as well as Articles of Association and the holders of sponsor shares as per law and rules are to vote for sponsor directors from amongst their sponsor holdings and the public share-holders vote for public share-holder director. And in such case, the company may take assistance of CDBL and the respective stock exchange and supply the accurate list to the election commission for holding smooth and fair election of directors of all the groups.

88. The next issue relating to record date, Mr Karim, the learned counsel submitted that the board of directors will fix record dates as per the notification and laws of SEC. Both Mr Huq and Mr Ahmed adopted the submission of Mr Karim. I also find that in any event Court cannot fix a record date, since it is the duty of board of director to fix a suitable record date as per law, further unless there is violation of law relating to fixing a record date or an purported action, more than a mere assumption leading to violation of law relating to fixing a record date, the Court cannot pass an order even directing the company to fix a record date, since the Court cannot act in vacuum. However, it is obligatory on the part of the board of directors of the respondent No. 1 company that it shall in compliance with relevant laws and SEC's Notifications fix a record dates for the AGMs in its due course of business and the record date which was earlier fixed by the board of directors in the year 2004 will be changed and a new record date will be fixed in accordance with the Companies Act as well as Notifications of the Securities and Exchange Commission.

In respect of appointment of auditor, this court cannot allow or appoint any auditor rather appointment of auditor is a prerogative of share-holders in general meeting. As such the auditor will be appointed in accordance with Companies Act as laws of Securities and Exchange Commission and other laws, if applicable in this regard.

90. Now I shall discuss whether a relief in any form can be granted under section 81(2) and section 85(3) of the Companies Act, 1994 in the garb of consequential and incidental order (অনুবর্তী ও আনুসাঙ্গিক). Under section 81(2) of the Companies Act, 1994, a consequential and incidental order can be passed while condoning a delay. Section 81(2) of the Companies Act, 1994 states as follows:—

“ বার্ষিক সাধারন সভা-(১) কোন কোম্পানী উপ-ধারা (১) এর বিধান পালনে ব্যর্থ হইলে কোম্পানীর যে কোন সদস্যেও আবেদনক্রমে আদালত উক্ত কোম্পানীর বার্ষিক সাধারন সভা আহবান করিতে অথবা আহবান করার নির্দেশ দিতে পারিবে এবং আদালত উক্ত সভা আহবান অনুষ্ঠান ও পরিচালনার জন্য যেরুপ সমীচীন করিবে সেইরুপ অনুবর্তী (consequential) ও আনুষংগিক (incidental)  আদেশ প্রদান করিতে পারিবে।”

91. The words 'consequential' and 'incidental' connote that the consequential order must have nexus to the cause of delay in holding AGM. Simply a delay in holding AGM has been condoned any order unrelated to the cause of delay cannot be passed for calling, holding and conducting the AGM. At the time of passing a consequential or incidental order for calling, holding and conducting the AGM, I am to be satisfied, (i) what is the cause of delay in holding the AGM, (ii) whether the cause or reasons for delay is still subsisting after condoning the delay, (iii) whether the consequential and incidental order intended to be passed shall diminish and overcome the said cause or reason for delay in holding AGM, which is subsisting after condonation of delay, (iv) whether the said consequential and incidental order shall be conducive for calling, holding and conducing the AGM and finally, (v) the said consequential and incidental order must not be contrary to any provision of the Companies Act, 1994, Articles of Association of the company or any provision of any other law applicable thereto. I do not find that any of the consequential or incidental reliefs as prayed by the petitioners were cause of delay in holding meeting. Therefore, such consequential or incidental reliefs as prayed by the petitioners cannot be granted ex debitio justitiae. Under section 85(3) of the Companies Act, 1994, a consequential or incidental order cannot be passed if and only if any meeting cannot be called in any approved manner or the same cannot be held in the manner prescribed by the Companies Act, 1994 or the Articles of Association of the company, then the Court can for the purpose of overcoming the impracticability in calling meeting or holding meeting may pass any consequential or incidental order along with the manner prescribed by the Court for calling, holding and conducting the meeting. This provision under section 85(3) of the Companies Act, 1994 is not inclusive of the provision under section 85(3) of the Companies Act, 1994. In the instant case, neither of the petitioners have alleged that the meeting could not be called in any approved manner, nor have they alleged that the meeting could not be held in the manner prescribed by the Companies Act, 1994 or the Articles of Association. Therefore, I find no scope to invoke the jurisdiction under section 85(3) of the Companies Act, 1994. However, in view of the threadbare discussion regarding the issues as agitated by all the parties I give guidelines in this respect hereinafter. This Court is inclined to pass the following directives.

92. Dr Zahir, the learned counsel, just before passing of the judgment, submitted before this Court for a direction to the company to sit with CDBL and Stock Exchange for ascertaining sponsor shares. But I find that since all the shares are ordinary shares there is no practicable purpose for sitting with CDBL and Stock Exchanges for ascertaining any nature of the shares. Only those who are sponsor share-holders are required to be ascertained. As I have found above the respondent No. 1 company has to ascertain those who are public subscribers and the rest of the members of the respondent No. 1 company including those whose names appear in the Articles of Association and still subsists as members of the company (except those who transferred their entire at any point of time) and also including those who were subscribers to the company immediately before IPO.

93. In the light of discussions made above, I have summarized my findings as follows:-

However, if required the company may trace and identify sponsor shares amongst holders of dematerialized shares of the company as per law and rules as well as Article of Association and the holders of sponsor shares as per law and rules are to vote for sponsor directors from amongst their sponsor holdings and the public share-holders vote for public share-holder director, and in such case, the company may take assistance of the CDBL and the respective stock exchanges and supply the accurate list of such share-holders to the Election Commission for holding smooth and fair election of directors of all the groups.
